newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia launches charm offensive for army reform.
newsitem.headline: Russia launches charm offensive for army reform.

text.p: The Russian government on Thursday launched a campaign to win over hearts and minds to a planned shakeup of the armed forces which conservative former officers warn could destabilise Russia.

Defence Minister Igor Sergeyev, instructed by President Boris Yeltsin to sell reform to more than a million disgruntled soldiers, told journalists he had already begun taking the message to the military and would meet reporters weekly.
"The morale situation in the armed forces is manageable but complicated," Sergeyev said, playing down opposition to the reforms which has been seized on by a group of former generals.

Yeltsin, faced with a budget crisis which has meant soldiers going hungry and officers not getting paid, has called for a big reduction in troop numbers and streamlining to cut out swathes of wasteful bureaucracy.
His ultimate goal, he says, is the creation of a mobile and modern force based on professional servicemen.
Sergeyev's predecessor Igor Rodionov is among several senior military officials who have savaged the reform plans and set up an organisation to defend what they call the army's interests.

The new defence minister gave his critics short shrift. "There's criticism and complaining...If there is criticism it must be objective," he said, saying no one had come up with a viable alternative to the cutbacks.
Sergeyev said a flood of calls to a hotline set up for the military had begun to dry up as the government fulfilled its pledge to pay off back wages.
"I think the mood is changing," he said. "If you don't believe us, sit in on one of the shifts taking the calls."
He said the state hoped to pay off the whole backlog of wages ahead of Yeltsin's September 1 target.

Sergeyev said he had talked several times to groups of army veterans -- "the most sensitive part of the armed forces" -- and this week met officers from the military space forces during the launch of a relief crew to the troubled Mir space station.
"Many officers, for they are after all clever lads, understand that any more crying and moaning will mean that everything will continue to collapse," he said.
A once-proud military machine has crumbled from a chronic cash crunch since the 1991 collapse of Soviet communism.

Officers often go months without pay and underfed recruits have been reduced to begging in the streets. Discipline in the ranks has weakened and suicides, thefts and bullying of young recruits by senior officers have become common.
Sergeyev dismissed suggestions the new organisation of his opponents could politicise the army. But the publicity campaign is a clear sign that the Kremlin is worried by the critics.

Last month, Yeltsin said in a nationwide radio address that his heart ached for hungry soldiers, officers whose wages were delayed and families stuck in cramped living quarters. He has also called on military experts to join the propaganda work.

On Thursday the Kremlin announced a new top level meeting on military reform to be addressed by Yeltsin, Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin, Sergeyev and other senior government and defence officials.
During the previous such meeting in May, cameras were allowed in to see Yeltsin angrily criticising Rodionov for not getting on with reforms. Within minutes he had sacked him.
Kremlin spokesman Sergei Yastrzhembsky said the August 22 meeting would be open to the media from start to finish.
